newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: US envoy says killings continuing in former Zaire.
newsitem.headline: US envoy says killings continuing in former Zaire.

text.p: A top U.S. aid official said on Tuesday that Washington believed massacres were continuing in the east of former Zaire and urged its new leader Laurent Kabila as well as Rwanda and Uganda to get their troops under control.

Brian Atwood, head of the U.S. Agency for International Development, said there was a "seemingly systematic effort" to cover up atrocities in the east of the country where Rwandan Hutu refugees are on the run from Tutsi-dominated former rebels who have blocked access to aid workers.

"We're not talking about the past tense. As we speak, there are still areas out of bounds for humanitarian workers in the eastern part of the Congo and we suspect that atrocities are now occuring," Atwood said.

"The real question is whether we can...try to stop the atrocities that are now occuring. We believe that these kinds of activities are still going on," he told a video news conference during a meeting of aid officials in the Swiss town of Wolfsberg, broadcast at the U.N. headquarters in Geneva.
"It's clear that Kabila now is in charge of this country and we are calling upon him to order the military forces under his command to abide by international standards."

Kabila's takeover last month as the self-proclaimed ruler of Africa's third largest country after a seven-month bush war has been tainted by widespread reports that his troops have been systematically killing Hutu refugees.

The United States has been supportive of Kabila and is a political and military ally of Rwanda and Uganda that have backed his rebels. But recently, it has recently been piling up pressure on the former rebels and Rwanda to stop the killings.
At the weekend, its ambassador to the United Nations, Bill Richardson, met Kabila who pledged to help a blocked U.N. probe into the massacres after failing to keep an earlier promise.
"We would like to see these areas opened up immediately so we can investigate the extent of these atrocities," Atwood said.
He said Washington had reports that forces from neighbouring Rwanda, where a Tutsi-dominated army holds sway, and from other countries in the region were in the region.
"All governments in the region including Rwanda, Burundi, Uganda, if they are in any way participating and if they have any knowledge, they should cooperate," he said.
The Hutus are the rump of some two million refugees who fled Rwanda in fear of reprisal for 1994's Hutu-led genocide and are collectively accused back home of taking part in the slaughters.

French television station TF1, in a documentary broadcast last week, interviewed refugees as well as a Zairean soldier who charged that Rwandan troops were gathering the Hutus in remote jungles, killing them and then burning their corpses.
The Zairean soldier named a Rwandan commander based in the eastern city of Kisangani whom he alleged had led the killings.

The privately-owned TF1 showed a still photograph of a heap of burnt corpses and interviewed Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees emerging from the forest, including one with an arm chopped off by a machete, who said they had witnessed killings by Rwandan Tutsi soldiers who spoke in their mother tongue.
There has been no independent confirmation of these reports in areas where aid workers have been denied access for weeks.
But senior aid officials say they fear tens of thousands of Hutu refugees might have been killed in recent weeks.
Many among an estimated 300,000 Rwandan Hutus whom the U.N. refugee agency says trekked deeper into Zaire in their run from the rebels remain unaccounted for.
